tier_reason: README runs Ada's own v4 Google Benchmark protocol via public code (benchmarks/run.sh + benchmarks/official_compare.cpp + benchmarks/official_bridge) against Ada pinned at b2c2d7f6 on the pinned 100,025-URL dataset, stating CPU (Apple M4), compilers (Rust 1.98.0, Apple Clang 21) and flags (run.sh: -O3 -DNDEBUG -mcpu=native -fomit-frame-pointer for C++, -C target-cpu=native for Rust, LTO off on both sides on macOS); raw JSON benchmarks/results/ada-b2c2d7f6-merged.json matches the README table exactly. corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.98.0 (opt-level=3, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, -C target-cpu=native) vs Apple Clang 21 building amalgamated Ada with -O3 -DNDEBUG -mcpu=native -fomit-frame-pointer (per benchmarks/run.sh); LTO matched by being OFF on both sides on macOS (on for both on Linux); ADA_USE_SIMDUTF=OFF, ADA_INCLUDE_URL_PATTERN=ON (Ada defaults)
corrections.caveats: Only one of the three headline operations (owned Url parse+href vs ada::url) is faster than Ada, and ada::url is Ada's heavier multi-string representation; Ada's own README examples all use ada::url_aggregator, and against it Lucid's UrlAggregator is slower (59.70 vs 57.26 ns/URL), as is can_parse (12.95 vs 11.25 ns). The README itself says Ada is ~1.04x faster for aggregator parsing and ~1.15x faster for can_parse and that 'parsing experiments did not show a dependable across-the-board gain'; the large setter speedups (up to ~174x) are Lucid before/after, not versus Ada. Single machine; Google Benchmark context records a 1-minute load average of ~4.5 during the run.

notes: Rejected as not-faster: the fastest representation of each library (UrlAggregator vs ada::url_aggregator) and can_parse both favor Ada in the project's own run, and the author explicitly disclaims a general parsing gain; the only win is against ada::url, Ada's heavier multi-string representation (all of Ada's README examples use ada::url_aggregator). Record's numbers, hardware, license (MIT), stars (4) and last commit (2026-09-07) are otherwise accurate; if the orchestrator keeps partial-win entries, tier A with the compiler_and_flags correction applies.

tier_reason: First-party microbenchmark only: public code (bench/bench.c3, bench/project.json with vendored picohttpparser at -O3 -msse4.2) but no CPU model (just "x86-64"), no c3c or C compiler version, and only rounded "typical" (~) figures with no raw output. It is neither peer-reviewed nor an independent suite, so B does not apply; the project's own code with partial methodology is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Typical (rounded) result on the bench page: the "no cb" run at ~99 ns/req (~10.1M req/s, ~113% of pico) vs picohttpparser at ~112 ns/req (~8.9M req/s), about 13% faster; the full callback-driven http::parser is at parity (~112 ns/req, ~99% of pico's throughput). In bench/bench.c3 the "no cb" run registers no callbacks at all (empty Settings, null context), so it extracts no method/path/header data while pico fills its method/path and 32-entry header array; the equal-output comparison is therefore parity, not a win. The page also says the SSE2 path is ~1.5x faster than pico's scalar (non-SSE4.2) build, with no numbers table for that claim
corrections.compiler_and_flags: c3c build at O3 (c3c version not stated); vendored picohttpparser compiled as a c-source of the same bench project with cflags -O3 -msse4.2 (C compiler not stated); http::parser uses 16-byte char[<16>] vectors (SSE2 on x86-64, NEON on aarch64 per README/src/simd.c3), no -march=native
corrections.caveats: Author's own bench README frames this as "indicative, not a verdict" given the different parser shapes (streaming push parser with per-token callbacks vs one-shot array filling) and also notes http::parser does extra body-framing work; the only faster number (~13%) comes from a run with no callbacks registered, which delivers no parsed fields while pico fills its header array, so at equal output the usable callback-driven parser is only at parity (~99% of pico); figures are rounded "typical" values from a single fixed hot-cache request, no raw output, no CPU model or compiler versions; repo history shows a single commit (authored 2026-06-27, committed 2026-08-02)

notes: Downgraded B to C: first-party benchmark code with partial methodology does not qualify for B. Numbers match the page, but the headline win is from a no-callback mode that does less output work than pico; the equal-work comparison is parity, so treat this as a thin/borderline claim.
